en: The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Part One:
The Section on the Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly. Chapter One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly.
It is said that when the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa:
Between the twin sāla trees, Ānanda sank into an ocean of grief; overcome by sorrow, he could not move forward.
Upāli first inquired: "What words should stand at the beginning of this sutra?
The Buddha’s teaching was thus recorded to be transmitted through all ages, past and present: "Thus have I heard."
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One...
At mealtime, he put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having gone through the city in succession begging for alms,
he returned to his original place.
When the meal was finished, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, arranged a seat, and sat down. 2.
The Second Chapter: Subhūti’s Request. At that time, the Elder Subhūti...
In the midst of the great assembly,
he rose from his seat,
bared his right shoulder, and placed his right knee upon the ground.
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas."
The Blessed One has well entrusted this to the bodhisattvas,
O son of good family, and to the daughter of good family.
Having resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
how should one dwell, and how should one subdue the mind?
The Buddha said:
Excellent, excellent,
Subhūti! It is just as you have said.
The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas and skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas.
Listen attentively now.
I shall now explain it for you:
sons and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"One should abide thus and thus subdue the mind.
Yes, World-Honored One;
we wish and desire to hear it."
3. The Section on the True Source of the Mahāyāna. Part Three. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner."
All classes of sentient beings whatsoever—
whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;
whether possessing form or formless.
Whether they possess perception, lack perception,
or possess neither perception nor non-perception,
I shall cause them all to enter nirvana without remainder and bring them to final liberation.
In this way, although he brings immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa,
in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span,
they are not a bodhisattva.
Maitreya spoke in verse:
When Śūnyatā-utpatti first requested instruction, The Sugata responded according to his capacity:
First, he answered how one should abide; Next, he taught how one should practice in this way.
Beings born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or by transformation— May all be gathered in by compassion and wisdom.
If one gives rise to the view of sentient beings, It is no different from seeking through attachment to signs.
Chapter Four: The Section on Sublime Practice Without Abiding. Furthermore, Subhūti, [the Tathāgata]...
One should practice giving without dwelling on any phenomenon; that is to say,
one should practice giving without dwelling on form.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena;
thus should a bodhisattva practice giving without dwelling upon signs.
Why is this? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs,
the resulting merit and virtue are inconceivable and immeasurable.
The Dānapāramitā of Giving. Maitreya’s verse says:
The gateway of giving encompasses the six perfections; The six perfections are subsumed within the three types of giving:
Giving material goods, giving fearlessness, and giving the Dharma; Let not sound and form interfere with one another.
Do not establish the two extremes; there is no need to settle upon a middle way.
If you seek the place of non-arising, turn away from objects and direct your gaze toward the mind.
This is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). Maitreya’s verse says:
Their ethical discipline (*śīla*) attains purity; for immeasurable eons, their causes have been conceptual constructions like hostile thieves. Their craving is as distant as the stars Shen and Chen;
though dwelling in desire, they are without desire; though abiding amidst the dust of the world, they are not defiled by the dust.
At the stage of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), one shall realize the body of the Dharma King.
Regarding the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*): Maitreya’s verse says:
"The mind that endures is like an illusion or a dream; The objects of insult are like the hair of a tortoise."
If one can constantly cultivate this contemplation, One will become even more steadfast when encountering hardships.
There is neither non-being nor being, Neither lowliness nor loftiness.
To extinguish the thieves of greed and hatred, One must wield the sword of wisdom.
Vīryapāramitā: Diligence. Maitreya’s verse says:
The stage of cultivation is named "Blazing" (Arciṣmatī), Because the light of wisdom spreads forth;
It dispels [delusions] within the mind through the two types of knowledge, And removes them from the three objects of emptiness.
Ignorance perishes moment by moment; through the realization that the mind is like space, one knows how to observe it without interruption.
How could this not lead to the unconditioned, the perfection of dhyāna, and meditative concentration? Maitreya’s verse says:
The river of dhyāna is pure as it follows the waves; The water of samādhi is clear as it pursues the ripples.
The spirit is clarified and the nature of awakening arises; Discursive thoughts cease and deluded sentiments are extinguished.
Pervasive conceptualization and false discrimination Have from the beginning been merely established by name.

If one realizes that the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) does not exist separately from the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), this is the wisdom of the perfection of insight (prajñāpāramitā). Maitreya’s verse says:
The lamp of wisdom is like the bright sun; The aggregates (skandha) and elements (dhātu) are like a city of Gandharvas (gandharvanagara).
When clarity arrives, darkness departs; there is no leisure for even a moment’s pause.
The deluded mind has not yet been extinguished, so the forms of self and others still appear.
When the light of wondrous wisdom shines perfectly, one attains nothing but the name of "emptiness."
Throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one fully cultivates the myriad practices;
having realized there is no self or person, one forever relies on the flow of the noble path.
Only then does one gradually realize the two kinds of emptiness, roaming freely at will within samādhi.
Having newly dwelt upon the Stage of Joy, he constantly delights in chasing away sorrow.
Subhūti, what do you think?
"Subhūti, can the space of the eastern direction be measured?
No, World-Honored One. "Subhūti," [the Buddha continued].
“Subhūti, can the space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured?
No, World-Honored One.
Subhūti, [it is thus.]
The Bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs;
his merit is likewise immeasurable and inconceivable, Subhūti.
"A Bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed.
Maitreya spoke in verse:
"If one discusses the merit of signless giving, it is truly immeasurable."
Practicing compassion to relieve the poor, one need not hope for karmic rewards;
The mental conduct of ordinary beings is inferior, so first let this be briefly extolled.
If you wish to know the appearance of giving (*dāna*), it is like space, pervading the ten directions.
5. The Section on Seeing According to Reality and as It Is, Part Five.
Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his physical marks?
"No, World-Honored One.
One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of physical marks. Why is this?"
The physical marks described by the Tathāgata are themselves not physical marks.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Whatever marks there may be, they are all illusory."
"If one sees that all marks are no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
Maitreya’s verse says:
"The Tathāgata displays his physical marks / To accord with the sentiments of worldly beings."
Fearing that people might give rise to the view of nihilism, I provisionally establish empty names and speak of thirty-two [marks]. Even at eighty, these are but hollow sounds;
the body is not the essence of awakening. Formlessness is the true form.
6. The Chapter on the Rarity of Right Faith. Chapter Six: The Rarity of Right Faith. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, is there any sentient being who, upon hearing such words and phrases as these, [will attain right faith?]"
“Do you truly have faith?
The Buddha told Subhūti,
“Do not speak thus.”
In the five hundred years following the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata,
there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit,
who are able to give rise to faith in these chapters and verses, regarding them as true.
Maitreya spoke in verse:
"The cause is profound, and the fruit is likewise profound; The principle is subtle and esoteric, difficult to fathom.
In the future age of the Dharma’s decline, I fear only that the Dharma will sink."
Śāriputra’s mind had not yet reached full understanding; hearing this teaching, he feared he could not bear its weight.
If one can believe in this Dharma, they must certainly be a person of awakened mind.
You should know that such a person has planted roots of goodness not under only one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas.
Those who have planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable tens of millions of buddhas,
and upon hearing these phrases,
give rise to even a single thought of pure faith— [for them, I shall act as their protector].
Subhūti, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees all these sentient beings who shall obtain such immeasurable merit.
Maitreya’s verse says:
When the faculty of faith gives rise to a single thought, All Buddhas are able to know it;
The cause was produced on this very day, And the fruit will be realized in the future.
The Three Vehicles have passed through many kalpas; The Six Perfections have long been practiced and applied.
Only when they have perfumed the formation of untainted seeds Are they designated as "inconceivable. Why is this so?
These sentient beings no longer have the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a being, or the notion of a life-span;
they have no notion of dharmas, nor do they have any notion of non-dharmas. Why is this?
If these sentient beings take up signs with their minds,
they will become attached to a self, a person, a being, and a life-span.
If one grasps at the characteristics of dharmas,
one is immediately attached to a self, a person, a sentient being,
and a life-span. Why is this?
If one grasps at the marks of what is not the Dharma,
one immediately becomes attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Maitreya states in verse:
The person is empty and phenomena are also empty; these two characteristics are fundamentally identical.
The parikalpita (imagined) nature is false conceptualization; the paratantra (dependent) nature is obstructed and lacks penetration.
The pariniṣpanna (perfected) nature is described as the ocean of consciousness, Whose cyclic flow is like drifting tumbleweeds.
If one wishes to realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
one must sever the traces of mental activity; therefore,
one should neither grasp at dharmas nor grasp at non-dharmas.
Maitreya’s verse says:
That which has causes is called a provisional designation; that which is signless is what the name pursues.
Existence and non-existence have no distinct essence; non-existence has no form within existence.
Existence and non-existence lack intrinsic nature; existence and non-existence arise falsely through the power of delusion, like an echo in a valley.
Therefore, do not cling to the sounds of existence and non-existence for this reason.
The Tathāgata has often said to you, bhikṣus:
"Know that my teaching of the Dharma is like the simile of the raft.
Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."
Maitreya spoke in verse:
To cross the river, one must use a raft; Upon reaching the shore, the boat is no longer needed.
When one knows that both person and phenomena are without self, What need is there to labor over the trap once the principle is realized?
Still drowning in the middle stream, who would discuss being on either side?
Whether existence or non-existence, if one grasps at either, the field of the mind is immediately defiled.
The Seventh Chapter: Neither Attainment nor Explanation. Subhūti, The Seventh Chapter: Neither Attainment nor Explanation. Subhūti, [continued:]
What do you think?
Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Or has the Tathāgata preached any dharma?
Subhūti said: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught,
there is no fixed dharma that is called 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'."
Furthermore, there is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can preach. Why is this?
All dharmas preached by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and inexpressible.
Neither dharma nor non-dharma.
Maitreya’s verse says:
Awakening transcends verbal expression; from the beginning, no one has ever attained it.
One must rely on the principle of the two emptinesses To realize the body of the Dharma King.
Mind and phenomena are both illusory; Non-attachment is what is called the truth.
If one awakens to that which is neither dharma nor non-dharma, One will roam at ease, transcending the six sense objects.
Why is this? Because all worthy and holy ones are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Maitreya’s verse says:
Grasping at both person and phenomena is called "clinging"; Upon realization, these two are non-active (unconditioned).
Bodhisattvas can realize them simultaneously; Śrāvakas abandon only one, not both.

Regarding the cognitive obscurations and afflictive obscurations, Within emptiness there is nothing upon which to rely; One who can constantly perform this contemplation Attains the noble concentration without doubt. What do you think?
If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift in alms.
"Would the merit obtained by this person be great?
Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Why is this? Because that merit is not the nature of merit;
therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.
Furthermore, if there should be someone who receives,
upholds, and even recites as little as a four-line verse from this sutra,
and explains it for others.
That merit would be superior to that.
Why is this? Subhūti, [it is because...]
All Buddhas and the Dharma of the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas—
all emerge from this sutra, Subhūti.
That which is called "Buddha-dharma" is not Buddha-dharma.
Maitreya spoke in verse:
Even if one were to fill the three thousandfold world system with jewels And offer them as a field of merit,
One accomplishes only tainted karma; Ultimately, one cannot leave behind the realms of humans and devas.
To uphold even four lines of this sutra And create a virtuous affinity with the Noble Ones, If one wishes to enter the sea of the unconditioned, One must board the ship of Prajñāpāramitā.
9. The Section on the Absence of All Marks, Number Nine. Subhūti, what do you think? Does a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) entertain such a thought as this:
[“I have attained the fruit of stream-entry”]?
"Have I attained the fruit of srotāpanna?
Subhūti replied, "No,
World-Honored One."
Why is this? The Srotāpanna is called "one who has entered the stream," yet there is nothing into which he enters;
he does not enter into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena.
This is called a srotāpanna. Subhūti, what do you think?
"Does a once-returner have this thought:
'I have attained the fruit of once-returning'? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
Why is this? A Sakṛdāgāmin is called 'one who comes back once more.'"
Yet in reality there is no coming or going;
this is called a Sakṛdāgāmin, Subhūti.
"What do you think? Does an Anāgāmin have this thought:
'I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin'?"
Subhūti said: "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?"
The Anāgāmin is called "one who does not come," yet in reality there is no coming;
therefore, he is named Anāgāmin.
Maitreya spoke in verse:
Having abandoned the state of ordinary beings and first attained the state of the noble ones, my afflictions have gradually become light and subtle;

having severed the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, and from the very beginning eliminated the perception of a self based on the body and the clinging to sensory objects, I now realize that [my former views] were not correct.
After seven more returns among gods and humans, one proceeds toward tranquility,
unaware of where one is headed. Subhūti, what do you think?
"Can an Arhat have this thought:
'Have I attained the path of Arhatship? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
Why is this? Because, in reality, there is no dharma that can be called 'Arhat'."
“World-Honored One,
if an Arhat were to have this thought:
‘I have attained the path of Arhatship.’”
"Then one would be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
World-Honored One,
the Buddha has said that among men I am the foremost in attaining the Samādhi of Non-Contention."
This is the foremost Arhat, detached from desire;
yet I do not harbor the thought:
"I have attained the path of Arhatship."
World-Honored One,
you would not say that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇya-dwelling,
because Subhūti truly has nothing to practice.
And the name Subhūti signifies one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
Maitreya spoke in verse:
Non-arising is itself non-ceasing; There is no self, nor is there a person.
Forever eliminating the hindrance of afflictions, Long bidding farewell to future existence,
objects vanish and the mind is extinguished. No longer arising as greed or hatred,
devoid of compassion yet possessing wisdom, Karma burns away as one alone abides in the Real.
10. The Section on Adorning the Pure Land. Chapter Ten: Adorning the Pure Land. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"What do you think?
When the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara..."
"Is there anything obtained regarding the Dharma?
"World-Honored One,
when the Tathāgata was in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha..."
In reality, there is nothing to be attained regarding phenomena.
Maitreya spoke in verse:
"In former times he was called Sudhana; Today he is named Śakra."
Observing that conditions and objects are illusory, The essence of consciousness is not the true nature of phenomena;

The Dharma-nature is neither cause nor effect. Realizing this according to principle, one receives the prediction of becoming a Buddha like Dīpaṃkara; How could one know that this was one’s former body?
Subhūti, what do you think?
Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields?
"No, World-Honored One.
Why is this? That which adorns the Buddha-lands is not truly adornment."
This is called adornment.
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
One should give rise to a pure mind in this way:
one should not dwell on forms when giving rise to the mind;
one should not dwell on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena when giving rise to the mind.
"One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere.
Maitreya’s verse says:
"Sweeping away the ground of the mind is called the cause for the Pure Land."
Whether in merit or wisdom, first abandon greed and hatred;
adorned with the transcendence of subject and object, untainted by self or person,
and by neither permanence nor annihilation, emerge in brilliant liberation from the clamor of the world.
Subhūti, it is as if there were a person whose body were like Sumeru,
the king of mountains. What do you think?
"Is this body great?
Subhūti replied, "It is exceedingly great, World-Honored One."
Why is this? The Buddha taught that what is not a body is called the "Great Body.
Maitreya spoke in verse:
Mount Sumeru is high and vast, used as a metaphor for the body of the Dharma King;
The seven treasures surround it in equal measure, and the six perfections stand side by side.
